brackets.notes: No derivations: under 1(j)(3)(B) each table is prescribed from its own 1(j)(2) base table, and 1(j)(3)(B)(iii) switches off 1(f)(8). The printed joint edges for 10% to 35% are exactly twice the single edges, and married-separate's 37% start is exactly half the joint 37% start, but that follows arithmetically from the 1(j)(2) base tables (built that way) and the $50/$25 rounding, not from a statute rule. The rates are written in 1(j)(2) and are not indexed. A qualifying surviving spouse uses married_joint (1(j)(2)(A)). Each status's schedule is indexed from its own 2018 base table: 26 U.S.C. 1(j)(3)(B)(iii) says subsection (f)(8) (the rule tying separate and single brackets to joint) shall not apply, and single and married filing separately round down to $25, the others to $50 (1(f)(7)(B), 1(j)(3)(B)(ii)). The 2018 base tables set the first five single and married filing separately edges at exactly half the joint edges, and rounding x down to $25 always equals half of 2x rounded down to $50, so those edges equal half the joint edges every year. A projection that derives them as joint x 0.5 gets the same figures; the 37% edges are indexed on their own either way.

start_age.notes: Born 1951 attains 72 in 2023 (after December 31, 2022), so 1951 is the first year under (I). Born 1959 satisfies both clauses as written (attains 73 in 2032, before January 1, 2033, and 74 in 2033, after December 31, 2032); recorded as 73, reading clause (I)'s explicit range as controlling (Publication 590-B (2025), PDF page 6, also gives age 73 to anyone who reaches 72 after December 31, 2022, without a 75 rule). Born 1960 or later: 75. People born before 1951 (age 72 or 70 1/2 under earlier law) are not covered: the current statute does not print their ages and the earlier-law boundary (reaching 70 1/2 after December 31, 2019) falls mid-year, which a birth-year row cannot hold.
